meaningEnglish: The Arranger (vyāsa from root vi + as = to separate, arrange; the one who arranged/compiled the Vedas)
historicalContext: Vyasa (also known as Veda Vyasa, Krishna Dvaipayana, or Badarayana) is the most celebrated figure in Hindu literary and philosophical tradition. He is traditionally credited with arranging the Vedas into four collections, composing the Mahabharata (including the Bhagavad Gita), the Brahma Sutras, and the 18 Mahapuranas.
explanation: Vyasa is considered a Chiranjivi (immortal) who periodically re-arranges the Vedas at the beginning of each cosmic age. He is the teacher of Paila (Rigveda), Vaishampayana (Yajurveda), Jaimini (Samaveda), and Sumantu (Atharvaveda). His son is Shuka, who narrates the Bhagavata Purana. Guru Purnima is traditionally celebrated as the anniversary of Vyasa.

sanskritPassages.sanskrit: व्यासाय विष्णुरूपाय व्यासरूपाय विष्णवे । नमो वै ब्रह्मनिधये वासिष्ठाय नमो नमः ॥
sanskritPassages.transliteration: vyāsāya viṣṇurūpāya vyāsarūpāya viṣṇave | namo vai brahmanidaye vāsiṣṭhāya namo namaḥ ||
sanskritPassages.translation: Salutation to Vyasa who is a form of Vishnu, and to Vishnu who is in the form of Vyasa. Salutation to him who is the treasury of Brahman, the descendant of Vasishtha.

sources.text: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1.57 (Vyasa compiles the Vedas)

meaningEnglish: Fallen into joined palms (pata = fallen; añjali = folded hands; the sage who fell from heaven into Anjali's hands, according to tradition)
historicalContext: Patanjali is traditionally credited with authorship of three important works: the Yoga Sutras (the definitive text on yoga philosophy), the Mahabhashya (the great commentary on Panini's grammar), and an Ayurveda text. Modern scholars generally believe these were written by different authors; the yoga Patanjali is dated approximately 200 BCE–200 CE.
explanation: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras codify the practice of yoga in 196 (or 195 by some counts) aphorisms across four chapters: Samadhi Pada, Sadhana Pada, Vibhuti Pada, and Kaivalya Pada. His definition of yoga as 'chitta vritti nirodha' (the cessation of mental modifications) became the basis of all subsequent yoga traditions. The Mahabhashya is the most authoritative commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi.

meaningEnglish: Descendant of Panin (a family name; the greatest grammarian of the ancient world)
historicalContext: Panini is the author of the Ashtadhyayi (c. 400–350 BCE), the most sophisticated grammatical treatise of the ancient world. He is believed to have been born in Shalatula, in the Gandhari region (modern Pakistan). His grammar describes Classical Sanskrit as it was spoken at his time.
explanation: Panini's Ashtadhyayi (Eight Chapters) consists of 3,959 sutras that generate the entire morphology of Sanskrit through a compact, recursive rule system. It uses metalinguistic markers (anubandhas/it-letters) with extraordinary economy. The grammar influenced not only Sanskrit scholarship but also modern formal linguistics — Ferdinand de Saussure and Noam Chomsky both acknowledged Panini's work.

sources.text: Ashtadhyayi 2.4.21 (a sample rule on nominal compounds)

meaningEnglish: Of the sacrificial enclosure (yajña = sacrifice; valka = bark; a family name associated with the sacrificial tradition)
historicalContext: Yajnavalkya is the greatest sage of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, presented as the most learned philosopher of his time. He is the teacher of the Shukla (White) Yajurveda tradition, having received the Vajasaneyi Samhita directly from the sun god (according to tradition). He is also the author of the Yajnavalkya Smriti (Dharmashastra).
explanation: Yajnavalkya's dialogues in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad with his wife Maitreyi, with the learned Gargi at the court of Janaka, and with other sages at the Brahmodya debate, represent the high point of Upanishadic philosophical discourse. His teaching of the Atman as the witness-consciousness (sakshi), his neti-neti method, and his declaration 'Aham Brahmasmi' (I am Brahman) are foundational for Advaita Vedanta.

meaningEnglish: Born of an anthill (valmīka = anthill; the sage who reportedly sat in meditation so long that an anthill grew around him)
historicalContext: Valmiki is the author of the Ramayana, the first poem (adikavya) in Sanskrit literature, making him the adi-kavi (first poet). He is traditionally depicted as a former hunter (Ratnakara) who reformed and became a sage. The Ramayana (c. 500–100 BCE) is composed in the Anushtubh metre.
explanation: Valmiki composed the Ramayana after witnessing a hunter kill a Krauncha bird and hearing the dying mate's lament. This sparked the first poetic utterance — a verse that emerged spontaneously in Anushtubh metre. His Ramayana established the narrative tradition of Sanskrit kavya (ornate poetry) and the ideals of dharmic character through Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and Hanuman.

sources.text: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 2 (Valmiki's first verse)

meaningEnglish: Most excellent, most wealthy (vasiṣṭha = superlative of vasu = good, wealthy; the best, the most distinguished)
historicalContext: Vasishtha is one of the Saptarishis (seven primordial sages) and is associated with the seventh book (Mandala 7) of the Rigveda, which is traditionally called the Vasishtha Mandala. He is the family priest (kula-guru) of the solar dynasty (Suryavamsha) and the preceptor of Rama in the Ramayana. The Yoga Vasishtha, a later philosophical text, is narrated in his name.
explanation: Vasishtha's rivalry with the royal sage Vishwamitra — narrated across Vedic and Puranic literature — is the central story of the tension between brahminical and kshatriya power. His cow Kamdhenu (Nandini) is a symbol of divine abundance. In the Ramayana, he presides over the coronation of Rama and guides the solar dynasty. As one of the Saptarishis, he is considered a mind-born son of Brahma.

sources.text: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 51–65 (Vasishtha and Vishwamitra conflict)

meaningEnglish: Friend of all (viśva = all, universe; mitra = friend; the sage who is a friend to all beings)
historicalContext: Vishwamitra is a unique figure in Hindu tradition — a king (Kaushika) who became a brahmarishi (brahmin sage) through extraordinary tapas. He is the author of the third Mandala of the Rigveda (Mandala 3), and traditionally attributed with composing the Gayatri Mantra (Rigveda 3.62.10), the most sacred mantra of the Hindu tradition. He is the guru of Rama and Lakshmana in the Ramayana.
explanation: Vishwamitra's transformation from king to brahmarishi is narrated in the Valmiki Ramayana and the Mahabharata. His rivalry with Vasishtha, his tapas to create a parallel heaven for the king Trishanku, and his role as the teacher of Rama — giving him divine weapons (astras) — are central to his legend. The Gayatri Mantra composed by him is recited by Hindus at dawn, noon, and dusk in the Sandhyavandana ritual.

sanskritPassages.sanskrit: तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं भर्गो देवस्य धीमहि । धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात् ॥
sanskritPassages.transliteration: tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi | dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ||
sanskritPassages.translation: We meditate on that excellent glory of the divine Savitri; may he inspire our intellects.

meaningEnglish: One who gives knowledge (nara = human being; da = giver; or nāra = water/knowledge; da = giver; the divine sage who gives spiritual knowledge)
historicalContext: Narada is a divine sage (Deva-Rishi) who appears throughout Hindu sacred literature — in the Rigveda, the Mahabharata, the Bhagavata Purana, the Ramayana, and many other texts. He is considered a mind-born son of Brahma and a devoted servant of Vishnu. The Narada Bhakti Sutras, a text on devotional practice attributed to him, is a foundational text of the Bhakti tradition.
explanation: Narada is the celestial wanderer who travels between the three worlds, playing the vina and chanting 'Narayana, Narayana'. He is both a messenger of the gods and a catalyst of events — his well-intentioned but often disruptive interventions are a staple of Puranic narrative. He is considered the foremost of devotees (bhaktas) and the transmitter of bhakti from the divine world to humanity. His instruction of Dhruva, Prahlada, and others in the Bhagavata Purana illustrates his role as a teacher of devotion.

meaningEnglish: The Tawny or Red-brown one (kapila = tawny, reddish-brown; a colour name used as a personal name)
historicalContext: Kapila is the founder of the Samkhya philosophical system, one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy. He is mentioned in the Bhagavad Gita (10.26) where Krishna declares 'Among perfected sages I am Kapila'. The Samkhya Sutras are attributed to him. In the Bhagavata Purana, Kapila appears as an avatar of Vishnu who teaches Samkhya to his mother Devahuti.
explanation: Kapila's Samkhya system is one of the oldest philosophical systems in Hindu thought, positing a radical dualism between Purusha (pure consciousness) and Prakriti (primordial matter). His analysis of the 25 tattvas (principles of reality) — including the three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) and the evolutionary development from Prakriti — became foundational for virtually all subsequent Hindu philosophy, including the Yoga school of Patanjali, Vedanta, and Tantra.

meaningEnglish: The teacher Madhva (madhva = honey-sweet; ācārya = teacher; the sweet teacher)
historicalContext: Madhvacharya (c. 1238–1317 CE), also known as Anandatirtha or Purnaprajna, was born in Pajaka near Udupi in coastal Karnataka. He is the founder of Dvaita Vedanta (dualistic Vedanta), also called Tattvavada (philosophy of reality). His principal works include the Brahma Sutra Bhashya, the Anuvyakhyana, and commentaries on ten principal Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Mahabharata.
explanation: Madhvacharya's Dvaita Vedanta posits five eternal distinctions (pancha bheda): between God and souls, between God and matter, between souls and matter, among souls, and among material entities. He established the Udupi Krishna temple and the system of eight mathas (monasteries) to manage its worship. He is considered a great debater who refuted Advaita Vedanta and other schools across India. His theology, asserting the supreme and irreducible reality of Vishnu, is the theological foundation of ISKCON's Vaishnava lineage through Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.
